sections.h2: Selling a house in Delaware, Ohio
sections.html:
Whether a Delaware owner hires an agent, goes it alone, or deals with a cash buyer, the deed ends up with the Delaware County Auditor and Recorder. Delaware is the county seat, set on the Olentangy River along U.S. Route 23 north of Columbus. Growth has been fast. The population is 46,636 for July 2025, up 12.9 percent from 41,297 in 2020.

Prices reflect that demand. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $318,400, and 64.7 percent of the 16,728 households own. Median gross rent is $1,286 and median monthly owner cost with a mortgage is $1,892. The city describes its draw as affordability, lower income taxes and small town living. The oldest housing sits around downtown and Ohio Wesleyan University, so expect buyers in those streets to ask about roofs, wiring and past repairs.

sections.h2: Which school district covers your address
sections.html:
Three public districts reach into the city, so one block can differ from the next. Delaware City, Olentangy Local and Buckeye Valley all serve parts of it. Buyers often start their search with a district in mind, so confirm the parcel before a listing names one.

Delaware City is the historic city district, with about 6,000 students. Olentangy Local is far larger at over 24,000 and covers a wide area across several jurisdictions. Buckeye Valley is the smallest, at around 2,300, and only part of it reaches the city.

Match the parcel against county records or ask the district before you promise anything in writing. A wrong guess in a listing can sour a buyer who chose the house for its schools.

One city department handles zoning, property maintenance and building review, and its building division is state-certified. Its FAQ answers several questions a seller or buyer will run into.

  • Structural, electrical or mechanical work likely needs a permit, and so do fences, decks, sheds, garages and additions. Patios do not.
  • Property line disputes are a civil matter between neighbors. The city suggests having the parcel surveyed.
  • Starting in 2026, contractors no longer need to register with the city.
  • All vehicles, including trailers, must be parked on a hard surface such as asphalt, concrete or existing gravel. New or expanded gravel parking is not allowed.
  • Signs in the right-of-way, tree lawns and on utility poles are prohibited, and code enforcement removes them.

If you built a deck or shed without a permit, ask the Building Division what it takes to close it out before a buyer's inspector finds it.

sections.h2: What happens if you ignore a violation notice
sections.html:
Formal violation notices are posted on the property. For a vacant property, the notice is mailed to the owner of record with the county auditor. When a deadline runs out, the city may make the fix itself and invoice the owner. Unpaid invoices can turn into a lien or ride on the tax bill, and charges through the city prosecutor are also possible.

Clear any notice before listing. A lien shows up in a title search, and it can hold up a closing or force a payoff from your proceeds. If you can't tell whether a notice was ever sent, call the city's code enforcement staff and ask for the address history. Pay or fix what is open, keep the receipt, and bring it to the closing so the title company can mark the item cleared.

sections.h2: Valuation, deeds and recording in Delaware County
sections.html:
For the 2026 triennial update, the Auditor's informal review is over. A formal complaint about a valuation goes to the Board of Revision, with filing open from January 1, 2027, through March 31, 2027, on the form listed with the Auditor's other forms. The Auditor's forms page also carries the Real Property Conveyance Fee Statement, DTE 100, and the office can quote the conveyance fee rate for your sale.

sections.h2: What Ohio requires a seller to disclose
sections.html:
Ohio's disclosure statute, R.C. 5302.30, applies to owners of homes with up to four units. The owner completes the state form and hands the buyer a signed copy. If the buyer first receives it, or an amended version, after signing a contract, the buyer can back out in writing within three business days. That right ends at the earlier of thirty days after acceptance or the closing.

Sales, land installment contracts, lease-options and exchanges all fall under it. Exclusions cover heirs who never occupied an inherited house for a year, plus transfers between spouses or to direct-line relatives. Fill the form out at listing time so there is no late amendment to cause trouble.

sections.h2: When a cash purchase helps a Delaware owner
sections.html:
A cash purchase helps when time or condition outweighs the last dollar of price. Deferred repairs, a code notice, sitting tenants or an unsettled estate can slow a listing. A buyer taking the house as it is removes showings and repair haggling.

Cash also suits owners who have already moved out. A vacant house draws code attention, and a posted notice is mailed to the owner of record, so a seller living elsewhere can miss a deadline. Selling quickly ends that exposure.

Before you accept a cash figure, compare it with what a listed sale would net after repairs, months of carrying costs and property tax that keeps accruing. Lay each buyer's written price, closing date and cost split next to the others.

sections.h2: How a Delaware sale moves from contract to closing
sections.html:
Once an offer is accepted, a title company runs a search of the property record. That is where a lien from an old city invoice, an unpermitted structure or a recording mistake would appear. Resolve anything it finds before the closing date, because the buyer's lender or attorney will want a clean title.

You sign the deed, the conveyance fee statement goes to the Auditor, and the deed is recorded with the Recorder at the fees above. Bring photo identification and any payoff letters to the signing. If you are selling an inherited house, bring the paperwork showing who holds title, since an unsettled estate is one of the most common reasons a closing stalls.

A cash buyer can often close faster because no lender sits in the middle. The state disclosure form, the title search and the deed recording still happen, so ask early who pays for each one.

faqs.q: What is the window to contest a Delaware County valuation?
faqs.a: The informal review for the 2026 triennial update is over. A formal complaint to the Board of Revision can be filed from January 1, 2027, to March 31, 2027, using the Auditor's own form.

faqs.q: Which home projects need a Delaware permit?
faqs.a: Fences, decks, sheds, garages and home additions need permits, and so does any structural, electrical or mechanical work. Patios do not. Ask the Building Division what is needed to close an unpermitted structure before listing.

faqs.q: What if I ignore a Delaware violation notice?
faqs.a: The city can fix the problem and bill you, and an unpaid bill may become a lien or join your property tax bill. It can also recommend charges through the city prosecutor.

faqs.q: Where is the Delaware County Recorder and what are its deed fees?
faqs.a: The Recorder's office is at 145 N. Union Street in Delaware. The fee is $39 for the first two pages, with a $5 preservation surcharge built in, and $8 per added page.

faqs.q: How do I tell which district my Delaware home is in?
faqs.a: It might be Delaware City, Olentangy Local or Buckeye Valley, since all three reach into the city. Match the parcel with county records or the district before naming one.
